clue.text: Reject public transport resistance in current sort of climate

indicators.note: to reject something is to send it back, so the word for public transport is turned around

parts.note: a bus is public transport

indicators.note: in puts the resistance symbol inside the word for current

parts.note: topical means current, of present interest
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Someone shuns buses and electricity in favour of the climate of a warm region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reject' seems to govern the whole phrase, but it only turns the vehicle round; 'current' means up to date, not electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: Subtropical describes the warm, humid kind of weather found just outside the tropics.

clue.text: Transport used by teacher importing endless coffee?

indicators.note: importing means bringing in, so the teacher's title takes the shortened coffee inside it

parts.note: pupils address a male teacher as sir

indicators.note: endless means the last letter of the coffee word is cut off

parts.note: decaf is decaffeinated coffee

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher is pictured needing a vehicle and smuggling in decaffeinated drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' drops the coffee's last letter before 'importing' sets it inside; the question mark flags that the teacher is merely a form of address.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidecar is a one-wheeled passenger carriage fixed to a motorcycle, a form of conveyance.

clue.text: Move resulting from golf in Cornish resort

indicators.note: in places the letter for golf inside the name of the resort

parts.note: Bude is a seaside town in Cornwall, south-west England
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A golfing holiday in Cornwall seems to prompt a change of location.
explanation.walkthrough: BUDE is a surfing resort on the north coast of Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: To budge is to shift position slightly, synonymous with stirring or shifting.

clue.text: Take a break — the setter's going back

parts.note: to recess is to adjourn or take a break
the setter refers to themself as I, so 'the setter's' becomes I'VE, short for I have

explanation.surface: A tired crossword compiler announces a pause and a return home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the setter's' is read as 'the setter has', giving I'VE; 'going back' looks like a reversal signal but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Recessive can mean tending to recede or withdraw, so moving backwards.

clue.text: Bacon may sell well? That's unlikely

parts.note: bacon comes from pigs
might is the past form of may, expressing possibility
goods that sell well fly off the shelves

explanation.surface: A butcher speculates that his bacon could be a bestseller, then doubts it.
explanation.walkthrough: Each word of the clue's first part gives one word of the phrase in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is said in response to something that will never happen, expressing scepticism.

clue.text: Entertainer caught working with one on panel

parts.note: C is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
a machine that is working is on
a juror is one member of a jury panel

explanation.surface: A performer is arrested while doing a stint of jury service.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjuror performs magic tricks to amuse an audience, a type of entertainer.

clue.text: Lawful impediment protecting US soldier

indicators.note: protecting means surrounding, so the impediment word wraps around the soldier

parts.note: a let is an obstruction, as in 'without let or hindrance'
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A legal obstacle shields an American serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: LET as a hindrance survives in tennis and in the passport phrase 'without let or hindrance'.
explanation.definitionFit: Legit is informal shorthand for legitimate, meaning allowed by law.

clue.text: Idiot priest's unfinished notice

indicators.note: unfinished means the last letter is dropped from the priest's title

parts.note: Father is the title of a Catholic priest
an ad is an advertisement, a notice

explanation.surface: A cleric's half-written church notice is dismissed as foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' applies only to the priest's title, not to the notice that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A fathead is a stupid person, a slang term for a dimwit.

clue.text: Inmate found outside a prison — that's incontestable

indicators.note: found outside means the inmate word sits around the other pieces

parts.note: a con is a convict, a prison inmate
stir is slang for prison

explanation.surface: A convict discovered beyond the jail walls is undeniable evidence of an escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found outside' reverses the surface: the inmate is outside only in the letters, wrapping the prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast-iron case or alibi is so solid it cannot be challenged.

clue.text: Figure pain mostly comes after coded broadcast

indicators.note: comes after places the shortened pain word behind the rearranged letters
broadcast means scattered, so the letters of coded are rearranged
mostly means the final letter of the pain word is dropped

parts.note: agony is severe pain

explanation.surface: Someone suffers after a coded message goes out on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges CODED as DODEC; 'mostly' cuts AGONY to AGON.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodecagon is a twelve-sided polygon, a geometric shape.

clue.text: Work hard replacing female with new allowance

indicators.note: replacing tells us one letter is swapped out for another in the hard-work word

parts.note: to graft is to toil

explanation.surface: Toiling earns a woman's replacement a new stipend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacing' swaps the F in GRAFT for N.
explanation.definitionFit: A grant is a sum of money awarded, such as a student allowance.

clue.text: Fold of cold fat — not good

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

indicators.note: not means the letter for good is taken away from the fat word

parts.note: grease is animal fat

explanation.surface: A roll of chilled fat is judged unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not good' reads as a verdict on the fat, but 'not' removes the letter for good.
explanation.definitionFit: A crease is a line made by folding cloth or paper.

clue.text: Teach those upset by reduction and focus on action

indicators.note: by means beside, so the reduction word stands next to the rearranged letters

parts.note: a cut is a reduction

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of teach those are jumbled

explanation.surface: Instructors are told to trim lessons and get pupils doing things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges TEACH THOSE into TO THE CHASE.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means skip the preliminaries and get to the point, from films jumping to the action.

clue.text: Withdraw material, then make public

parts.note: rep is a ribbed fabric
to air an opinion is to make it public

explanation.surface: Someone takes back some cloth and then announces it.
explanation.walkthrough: REP is a corded fabric used in upholstery.
explanation.definitionFit: To repair to a place is formally to retire or go there, as in repairing to the drawing room.

clue.text: Scheme to accommodate a church minister's first appointee

indicators.note: to accommodate means to hold inside, so the scheme word wraps the other pieces

parts.note: a plan is a scheme
CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: first takes just the opening letter of minister's

explanation.surface: A plot to house a clergyman's first nominee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to accommodate' takes in three pieces at once, including the minister's initial.
explanation.definitionFit: A placeman is someone given an official post as a reward for political loyalty.

clue.text: Got dried off, ready for bed?

indicators.note: off means gone bad or wrong, so the letters of got dried are rearranged

explanation.surface: After a bath someone towels down and is set for sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' signals rearranging GOT DRIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Dog-tired means utterly exhausted, so sleepy enough to need a night's rest.

clue.text: Excessively stupid, grabbing power tool for clearing gaps

parts.note: too means excessively

indicators.note: grabbing means holding inside, so the stupid word takes in the power letter

parts.note: thick means stupid
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: An overly dim person seizes an electric tool to fill holes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grabbing' puts P inside THICK.
explanation.definitionFit: A toothpick removes food lodged in the spaces between teeth.

clue.text: See 4
Offsets evil business taking precedence

indicators.note: taking precedence means going first, so the business word comes before the evil one

parts.note: trade is business or commerce
sin is evil

explanation.surface: Accounts are balanced when wicked commerce is put first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking precedence' tells the solver that the business word, though second in the clue, comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To trade in an old car is to offset its value against the price of a new one.

clue.text: Claret blended with last of the syrup

indicators.note: blended means mixed together, so the letters of claret are rearranged
last of takes the final letter of the

explanation.surface: Red wine is mixed with the dregs of a sweet syrup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blended' rearranges CLARET as TREACL; 'last of the' adds E.
explanation.definitionFit: Treacle is a thick dark syrup made during sugar refining.

clue.text: Eschewing New York, Tennyson composed such lines

indicators.note: eschewing means avoiding, so the letters for New York are left out of the poet's name
composed means put together anew, so the remaining letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The Victorian poet avoids America while writing verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eschewing' removes NY from TENNYSON; 'composed' rearranges TESON to SONNET. The definition leans on the clue: Tennyson wrote such lines.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonnet is a fourteen-line poem, the kind of verse a poet like Tennyson composed.

clue.text: This oddly covers a loan for the final part

indicators.note: covers means the two odd letters sit either side of the a
oddly takes the first and third letters of this

parts.note: to lend is to loan

explanation.surface: A borrowing agreement oddly covers the last section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' gives the first and third letters of This; 'covers' sets the a between that pair before the loan word follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The tail end is the last portion of something, such as a queue or a season.

clue.text: Vision of cardinal welcoming positive response

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in, so the number word holds the positive response

parts.note: eight is a cardinal number
yes is a positive response

explanation.surface: A prince of the church greets an affirmative answer with a vision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cardinal' suggests a churchman, but here it means a cardinal number.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyesight is the faculty of seeing, synonymous with sight.

clue.text: Thoughts from assistants finding answer further down

indicators.note: further down in a down clue means the letter moves lower, nearer the end of the word for assistants

parts.note: aides are assistants

explanation.surface: Helpers come up with a solution lower down the page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'further down' moves the A in AIDES from first to fourth place.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideas are notions or concepts, products of thinking.

clue.text: Butcher's fine cuts hit us badly

indicators.note: cuts means slices into, so the fine letter goes inside the rearranged letters
badly means the letters of hit us are jumbled

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine on pencils

explanation.surface: A butcher's penalty ruinously slashes a business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher's' is rhyming slang: butcher's hook = look. 'badly' rearranges HIT US to SHUTI; 'cuts' puts F inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Shufti is British slang for a quick look, so both words mean a glance.

clue.text: Fine cotton that's used to start a fire

definitions.text: that's used to start a fire

parts.note: lint is a soft cotton or linen fabric used for dressings

explanation.surface: Delicate cotton serves as kindling.
explanation.walkthrough: Lint is also fluff, which suits the surface's tinder idea.
explanation.definitionFit: Flint is a hard stone struck against steel to make sparks for lighting.

clue.text: Repeat part of speech (off-the-record)

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An unattributed remark is repeated from a segment of a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To echo is to repeat what someone else has said.

clue.text: See 12
Copy of dossier about dodgy claims missing line

indicators.note: about means around, so the dossier word goes round the rearranged letters

parts.note: a file is a dossier

indicators.note: dodgy means unsound, so the letters of claims are rearranged
missing means the line letter is left out of claims

explanation.surface: A duplicate dossier concerns suspect claims with one line absent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing line' and 'dodgy' leave ACSIM from claims; 'about' splits the dossier word around it after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A facsimile is an exact reproduction of a document.

clue.text: Reprimand journalist after broadcaster shot up

indicators.note: after places the reprimand and journalist pieces behind the broadcaster

parts.note: Sky is a British TV broadcaster
a rocket is a severe reprimand in British slang
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A TV company scolds a newspaper man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reprimand' is British slang 'a rocket'; Sky is a British satellite broadcaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Skyrocketed means rose rapidly, as prices or rockets do.
